content.content:
Never-Sold: "We are a few dozen, in Blackrose and round it, and we get the held out. Our oath is three words. Bones go home. An Owing stands on three legs. The first is the count, which the holder keeps under lock. The second is the word that says it stands. The third is the hand, someone paid to fetch a runaway back. Take one leg away and the whole Owing falls. We take them with a key lifted off a belt, a lock opened in the dark, a keeper faced down at his own door and a fetcher met on a channel bank. Nobody else is going to do it."

content.content:
Never-Sold: "Her name is Rows-For-Another. Eleven years ago she holed a boat on the Tulm-Varo estate north of town, and the estate's keeper set her four nushmeekos, four months of work. She owes more now than she did then. I give you a leaf in my own hand, five picks and 100 gold. Her leaf lies in the estate's count-box: take it, and leave mine in its place. The gold is the first price. By custom an Owing paid at its first price is closed for good, and Hulm-Tei, the keeper, has refused it from me twice. He may not refuse it from someone who brings more than coin. There are three doors, and any one will do: rob the box, make Hulm-Tei strike her leaf himself, or get past Brings-Them-Back, the fetcher on the channel. Each door costs. Seen at the box, you are a thief on the estate's ground. Kill the fetcher and you have a death on you. Go north past the farm with its cattle and its big house, to the channel bank beyond. Hear from Rows-For-Another how she is held."

content.content:
Never-Sold: "There are no jails in Black Marsh. When a person does a wrong, they pay it in work, in nushmeekos. A nushmeeko is one month of work that nobody thanks you for, and once it is worked off nobody mentions it again. In the south that has gone bad. Whoever holds the estate or the landing does the reckoning, and he writes food, breakage and sickness onto the months until they never end. A person can be born owing and die owing. I was born owing, and I got out. That is why I do what I do."

content.content:
Rows-For-Another: "I holed a Tulm-Varo boat eleven years ago, and the Owing for it, the work I must do to pay, is not ended yet. The tree my tribe is hatched under is the Hist, and I have not stood under mine in all that time. Look at my arms. My colour is still mine, but every morning I look for the day it fades, and I think of walking home grey, with my own kin asking whose child I am. Three things hold me. The keeper, Hulm-Tei, stands in the big house on the farm by the cattle and carries the key to the count-box in it, where my leaf lies, the page that says what I owe. His word is the second: by custom he may take the first price and close an Owing for good, and he has refused it. The third is Brings-Them-Back. He fetches runaways on this channel for a head-price, and he stands where it runs on north of this bank. He knows the way to my tree, so if I run while he lives, I can never go home. Each way out has its cost, as far as I know it. Lift my leaf from the box and my Owing goes with it. What that costs the keeper I cannot say. Ask for his word and you must move him, and he will tell you every line on my leaf is true: four months, then my food, then a fever. He is right. It has outgrown me. The channel costs most: buy the fetcher and he looks away, yet still knows my tree; kill him and I may go home, with a man dead for my sake. That is why I want my Owing closed, not fled. When the channel is clear, because he is dead or has agreed to look away, come and tell me."
Objective completed: Speak to Rows-For-Another on the channel bank north of Blackrose.
Journal entry (Four Months for a Boat): Rows-For-Another told me what holds her: her leaf in the count-box inside the estate house, whose key the keeper Hulm-Tei wears; Hulm-Tei's word, which could close the Owing; and Brings-Them-Back, the fetcher on the channel north of the bank, who knows the way to her home tree. I'm to break any one of the three.
New objective: End Rows-For-Another's Owing: take her leaf from the count-box (lift Hulm-Tei's key, or pick the lock); or win Hulm-Tei's word; or clear the channel of Brings-Them-Back.

content.content:
Hulm-Tei: "I am Hulm-Tei, keeper of the count for the Tulm-Varo, who hold this farm. The count is the written account of what each hand on this farm owes. My mistress, who winters in Gideon, far from here, leaves it to me. I was hatched owing on this ground. A debt came with my egg, and the work that pays a debt is called an Owing. Every line I write on a hand's leaf, the page that holds the debt, is true. Forty people eat because the boats go out, and the hands are the ones who row them. When the count is short at the reckoning, when the season's count is closed, the shortage is written on me. So I am hard about a line, and I will not be shamed for it. The keeper before me wrote smaller than I do, and more exactly. You will see it in the first lines of the oldest leaves in the count-box. I stand in this house, the big one on the farm by the cattle, because the box is in it."

content.text:
I finished the quest "Four Months for a Boat". Rows-For-Another is free, and my journal shows nothing active, so I ended the game and gave my take.

- **Persuasion failed.** Hulm-Tei refused the 100-gold first price even when I tried to talk him round.
- **Taking the leaf worked.** I lifted his key unseen, opened the count-box, took Rows-For-Another's leaf and also took the keeper's own leaf.
- **Hulm-Tei took his leaf back.** I gave it to him with the 100 gold, and he struck her leaf himself.
- **The cost.** Hulm-Tei leaves the estate, and a dozen farm hands will share what she owed without ever knowing why. Never-Sold said she would have chosen the keeper to pay instead.
- **Reward.** She paid me 100 gold and ten lockpicks and made me a Chainbreaker. She also admitted she knew about the keeper's leaf before she sent me.

I never told Rows-For-Another herself that she is free. Nothing new started after the quest, so I stopped.
